# Motion Style Atlas: Regeneration Prompts

Each of the 277 styles below has two prompts:

- **Build prompt**: a full director's brief. Give it to Claude or another coding model to make a procedural 10-second film (Canvas/WebGL + Web Audio), or hand it to a motion designer as a creative brief.
- **Video-model prompt**: a short descriptive prompt for text-to-video tools.

To match the atlas exactly, attach the reference film from `videos/` and, for coding models, `js/engine.js` (the shared timing, easing and audio helpers). Every film in the atlas follows the same contract: `MG.film({ id, dur, meta, setup, draw(c, t, W, H, st), score(A) })`.

## 01 · Visual Music
*After John Whitney · 1921 — · Graphic Design & Historical*

Reference film: `videos/whitney.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Visual Music** (After John Whitney, 1921 —; family: Graphic Design & Historical).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Abstract-film pioneers Ruttmann and Fischinger "played" music with shapes. In 1960 John Whitney founded Motion Graphics Inc. and gave the field its name.
- Study these reference works: An Optical Poem (1938) · Catalog (1961) · Arabesque (1975)
- Motion DNA: Each element rotates at a speed proportional to its index; patterns lock whenever the speeds form whole-number ratios.
- Visual DNA: Glowing points on black, rosette symmetry, warm-to-cool hue ramp, almost no type.
- Signature transitions: Symmetry lock, collapse to a line
- Key techniques: Differential motion, Symmetry locks, Additive trails

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Differential motion, Symmetry locks, Additive trails).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Differential motion and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "VISUAL MUSIC", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: Canvas 2D, Processing, TouchDesigner. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Make each frame a pure function of time t, and use seeded randomness so any frame can be re-rendered exactly.
- Sound is part of the film: write a score and sound effects whose hits land exactly on the visual events. Keep peaks below 0 dBFS.
- Use the style's real palette, materials and typography, and include at least one detail that only this style would have.
- Loopable: make the last frame cut cleanly back to the first.
- Reproducibility note: Fully procedural.

DELIVER: the film (or code that renders it), plus a beat sheet listing each event with its timing.
```

### Video-model prompt (Sora / Runway / Kling / Veo)
```text
10-second Visual Music motion-graphics film (After John Whitney). Visual style: glowing points on black, rosette symmetry, warm-to-cool hue ramp, almost no type. Motion: each element rotates at a speed proportional to its index; patterns lock whenever the speeds form whole-number ratios. Signature moves: differential motion, symmetry locks, additive trails; transitions: symmetry lock, collapse to a line. In the tradition of An Optical Poem (1938) · Catalog (1961) · Arabesque (1975). Award-winning motion design, crisp detail, 16:9, 1920×1080. It ends on a clean title card reading "VISUAL MUSIC". Punchy sound design synced to every cut.
```

## 04 · Art Deco Motion
*Machine-age Glamour · 1925 — · Graphic Design & Historical*

Reference film: `videos/artdeco.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Art Deco Motion** (Machine-age Glamour, 1925 —; family: Graphic Design & Historical).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Named after the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs in Paris, Art Deco fused Cubist geometry, Egyptian and Aztec motifs and machine-age streamlining; Cassandre's posters and New York's setback skyscrapers made it the look of luxury and speed.
- Study these reference works: Chrysler Building crown (William Van Alen, 1930) · "Normandie" poster (A. M. Cassandre, 1935) · "Étoile du Nord" poster (Cassandre, 1927) · Radio City Music Hall (1932) · The Great Gatsby titles (2013)
- Motion DNA: Everything grows from one axis in mirrored pairs: a plumb line falls, rays fan out on the beat, arches stack like a fanfare, lines streak outward, and a sheen sweeps the gold.
- Visual DNA: Gold on black: sunbursts, stepped ziggurats, chevrons, scallop fans and streamlines in strict bilateral symmetry, with high-contrast inline capitals.
- Signature transitions: Line draw-on from the axis, symmetrical bloom, mask-rise reveals, specular sweeps, slow camera pull-out.
- Key techniques: Mirror-symmetric draw-on of every ornament, Metallic gold gradients with a travelling sheen, Inline display type rising through a horizon mask, Additive bloom on gold line-work

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Mirror-symmetric draw-on of every ornament, Metallic gold gradients with a travelling sheen, Inline display type rising through a horizon mask, Additive bloom on gold line-work).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Mirror-symmetric draw-on of every ornament and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "ART DECO MOTION", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: After Effects, SVG, Canvas 2D. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Make each frame a pure function of time t, and use seeded randomness so any frame can be re-rendered exactly.
- Sound is part of the film: write a score and sound effects whose hits land exactly on the visual events. Keep peaks below 0 dBFS.
- Use the style's real palette, materials and typography, and include at least one detail that only this style would have.
- One-shot: it does not need to loop.
- Reproducibility note: Fully procedural.

DELIVER: the film (or code that renders it), plus a beat sheet listing each event with its timing.
```

## 05 · Constructivism
*Art into Life, Type as a Weapon · 1919 — · Graphic Design & Historical*

Reference film: `videos/constructivism.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Constructivism** (Art into Life, Type as a Weapon, 1919 —; family: Graphic Design & Historical).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Born in revolutionary Russia, Constructivism rejected easel art for agit-prop, posters and film; El Lissitzky, Alexander Rodchenko and the Stenberg brothers built images from diagonals, flat red and black, sans-serif type and photomontage.
- Study these reference works: "Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge" (El Lissitzky, 1919) · Lengiz "Books" poster (Rodchenko, 1924) · "Kino-Eye" poster (Rodchenko, 1924) · "Man with a Movie Camera" poster (Stenberg brothers, 1929) · "Iron Foundry" (Mosolov, 1926–28)
- Motion DNA: Nothing drifts: a wedge strikes, words slam on steep angles, rays burst, the loudspeaker recoils with each shout, and the camera whips and rolls between blocks before pulling back to the poster.
- Visual DNA: Red, black and raw cream; wedge, circle and bar; condensed sans set on diagonals; halftone eye and radiating lines on letterpress paper.
- Signature transitions: Whip pans with motion blur, camera rolls, red flash on impact, slam-in scale stamps, final pull-back reveal.
- Key techniques: Steep diagonal camera with whip-pan blur, Procedural halftone photomontage, Hard slams with overshoot and shake, Hand-cut edges and print mottling

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Steep diagonal camera with whip-pan blur, Procedural halftone photomontage, Hard slams with overshoot and shake, Hand-cut edges and print mottling).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Steep diagonal camera with whip-pan blur and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "CONSTRUCTIVISM", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: After Effects, Canvas 2D, Web Audio. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Make each frame a pure function of time t, and use seeded randomness so any frame can be re-rendered exactly.
- Sound is part of the film: write a score and sound effects whose hits land exactly on the visual events. Keep peaks below 0 dBFS.
- Use the style's real palette, materials and typography, and include at least one detail that only this style would have.
- One-shot: it does not need to loop.
- Reproducibility note: Fully procedural.

DELIVER: the film (or code that renders it), plus a beat sheet listing each event with its timing.
```

## 06 · Psychedelic 60s
*Liquid Light and Melting Letters · 1966 — · Graphic Design & Historical*

Reference film: `videos/psychedelic.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Psychedelic 60s** (Liquid Light and Melting Letters, 1966 —; family: Graphic Design & Historical).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: In San Francisco's 1966–68 dance-hall scene, Wes Wilson, Victor Moscoso and others made concert posters whose letters swelled to fill shapes and whose complementary colours vibrated; liquid light shows of dyed oil on overhead projectors played behind the bands, and Peter Max and "Yellow Submarine" took the look to pop.
- Study these reference works: Fillmore Auditorium posters (Wes Wilson, 1966–67) · "Neon Rose" series (Victor Moscoso, 1967) · "Yellow Submarine" (Heinz Edelmann, 1968) · Peter Max posters (late 1960s) · Joshua Light Show at the Fillmore East (1968 —)
- Motion DNA: Nothing is rigid: colour pools, folds, spirals and cycles on the beat, flowers spring open, and letters flow like hot wax until they settle into a swollen, legible shape.
- Visual DNA: Same-value complementary colours that vibrate, liquid dye blobs, op-art spirals, outlined flowers and hand-lettering stretched to fill a balloon.
- Signature transitions: Kaleidoscope fold, spiral iris, liquid-edged radial wipes, zoom-through tunnel, melt-in with drips.
- Key techniques: Subtractive dye metaballs on a projector hotspot, Kaleidoscope fold and log-spiral op-art, Per-pixel shape-filling text warp, Blur-threshold "goo" lettering

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Subtractive dye metaballs on a projector hotspot, Kaleidoscope fold and log-spiral op-art, Per-pixel shape-filling text warp, Blur-threshold "goo" lettering).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Subtractive dye metaballs on a projector hotspot and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "PSYCHEDELIC 60S", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: Canvas 2D, Liquid light show, GLSL. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Make each frame a pure function of time t, and use seeded randomness so any frame can be re-rendered exactly.
- Sound is part of the film: write a score and sound effects whose hits land exactly on the visual events. Keep peaks below 0 dBFS.
- Use the style's real palette, materials and typography, and include at least one detail that only this style would have.
- One-shot: it does not need to loop.
- Reproducibility note: Fully procedural.

DELIVER: the film (or code that renders it), plus a beat sheet listing each event with its timing.
```

## 07 · Op Art Kinetic
*Optical Vibration · 1960 — · Graphic Design & Historical*

Reference film: `videos/opart.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Op Art Kinetic** (Optical Vibration, 1960 —; family: Graphic Design & Historical).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Op (optical) art used precise black-and-white geometry to make flat paintings appear to move, swell and flicker on the retina; Bridget Riley and Victor Vasarely led it, and MoMA’s 1965 exhibition The Responsive Eye made it a global sensation.
- Study these reference works: Movement in Squares (Bridget Riley, 1961) · Current (Bridget Riley, 1964) · Fall (Bridget Riley, 1963) · Vega series (Victor Vasarely, 1957—) · The Responsive Eye (MoMA, 1965)
- Motion DNA: Precise, vibrating motion: periods collapse in clicks, lines undulate, squares fold and bulge, and two ring fields beat against each other until they lock still.
- Visual DNA: Pure black and white: dense parallel stripes, compressed checkerboards, spherical bulges and concentric rings, no colour and no texture.
- Signature transitions: Period-doubling, slanted wipe, fold relax into bulge, iris to moiré, ring flattening to stripes, phase-shift reveal
- Key techniques: Analytic anti-aliased stripe fields, Moiré interference, Lens-warped checkerboards

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Analytic anti-aliased stripe fields, Moiré interference, Lens-warped checkerboards).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Analytic anti-aliased stripe fields and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "OP ART KINETIC", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: GLSL, Canvas 2D, After Effects. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Make each frame a pure function of time t, and use seeded randomness so any frame can be re-rendered exactly.
- Sound is part of the film: write a score and sound effects whose hits land exactly on the visual events. Keep peaks below 0 dBFS.
- Use the style's real palette, materials and typography, and include at least one detail that only this style would have.
- One-shot: it does not need to loop.
- Reproducibility note: Fully procedural.

DELIVER: the film (or code that renders it), plus a beat sheet listing each event with its timing.
```

## 08 · Memphis Design
*Postmodern Pop Pattern · 1981 — 1988 · Graphic Design & Historical*

Reference film: `videos/memphis.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Memphis Design** (Postmodern Pop Pattern, 1981 — 1988; family: Graphic Design & Historical).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: A Milan design collective founded by Ettore Sottsass in December 1980 and launched at the 1981 Salone del Mobile; it threw out good-taste modernism for laminate patterns, clashing colours and toy-like geometry, and its look later flooded 1980s TV graphics and packaging.
- Study these reference works: Carlton room divider (Ettore Sottsass, 1981) · Bacterio laminate (Ettore Sottsass, 1978) · Gabon & Zambia patterns (Nathalie Du Pasquier, 1982) · Super lamp (Martine Bedin, 1981) · Saved by the Bell title graphics (NBC, 1989)
- Motion DNA: Bouncy and overshoot-heavy: shapes drop with squash and stretch, slide in past their mark and spring back, all locked to a synth-pop beat.
- Visual DNA: Pastel and primary clashes, black-and-white laminate patterns, squiggles, confetti terrazzo, zig-zags, cylinders, cones and half-moons with hard black shadows.
- Signature transitions: Pattern panel slide, spring pop, drop-and-bounce, palette clash flash, confetti burst
- Key techniques: Laminate patterns: squiggle, terrazzo, grid, dots, Hard offset shadows & black keylines, Squash-and-stretch bounce stacking

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Laminate patterns: squiggle, terrazzo, grid, dots, Hard offset shadows & black keylines, Squash-and-stretch bounce stacking).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Laminate patterns: squiggle, terrazzo, grid, dots and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "MEMPHIS DESIGN", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: After Effects, Canvas 2D, Illustrator. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Make each frame a pure function of time t, and use seeded randomness so any frame can be re-rendered exactly.

- Lineage: Riso Kagaku of Tokyo released its first Risograph digital duplicator in 1986: a thermal master stencil is burned and wrapped on an ink drum, and each colour is a separate pass of soy-based ink. Built for schools and offices, the machines were adopted by zine makers and art-book presses in the 2010s, and riso-printed flipbooks and frame-by-frame print animations, often faked digitally, turned its grain, fluorescent pink and loose registration into a motion look.

- Motion DNA: Animated on twos, and every drawing is a separate pull: the plates shift a few pixels and the grain changes each frame, so even a still image boils; colour arrives one drum pass at a time.

- Signature transitions: Drum pass wipe, overprint build-up, misregistration storm, paper jam smear, sheet eject and feed
- Key techniques: One offscreen plate per ink, multiplied, Per-frame misregistration, Stochastic ink coverage mask, Rotated halftone screens

- Lineage: Art Nouveau took its name from Siegfried Bing’s Paris shop, the Maison de l’Art Nouveau (1895), and spread across Europe as Jugendstil, Secession and Modernisme: a total style that let one living line run through posters, ironwork, glass, furniture and buildings. - Motion DNA: Nothing is placed, everything grows: stalks rise and bow over, shoots uncurl, leaves unfold along vines, hair pours out in waves that travel down each strand and wind into spirals, while the whole poster breathes with a slow sway and the light moves through the glass.

- Signature transitions: Needle-bundle wipe, train rush-through, figure stride-in, word slams from every side, black diagonal title band
- Key techniques: Chronophotographic echoes, Force-line rays and planes, Words-in-freedom slams

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Neon signs are hand-bent glass tubes filled with low-pressure gas and lit by a high-voltage transformer: neon glows red-orange, argon with a drop of mercury glows blue, and phosphor coatings give every other colour. Georges Claude showed the first neon tubes in Paris in 1910 and the signs reached America in 1923; by the 1950s the Young Electric Sign Company had turned Las Vegas into a street of animated cabinets, chaser bulbs and sequenced arrows, and Hong Kong’s Nathan Road hung its signs in canyons over the traffic. The Neon Museum in Las Vegas now keeps the retired ones.
- Study these reference works: Neon tube lighting (Georges Claude, Paris Motor Show, 1910) · Vegas Vic (Young Electric Sign Company, 1951) · Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign (Betty Willis, 1959) · The Neon Museum, Las Vegas (opened 2012)
- Motion DNA: Nothing slides: light is the only thing that moves. Tubes strike with a stutter and argon warms up slowly, chaser bulbs step round the cabinet, the arrow builds segment by segment and blanks, a three-state figure jumps between fixed poses, a faulty tube sputters and dies, while rain falls and the reflections ripple in the puddles.
- Visual DNA: Saturated pink, argon blue, red, yellow and turquoise light with white-hot tube cores and wide soft halos, against wet red brick and dark pavement; script and block lettering in a single continuous tube, electrodes and glass standoffs, a painted Googie sheet-metal cabinet ringed with incandescent bulbs.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: A camera photographs artwork through a narrow moving slit during one long exposure per frame, so each part of the image records a different moment. John Whitney explored it in the early 1960s; Douglas Trumbull built a slit-scan machine for the Stargate sequence of Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968). Bernard Lodge used it for Doctor Who's 1973 time tunnel, and digital "time-slice" video revived it by giving every row or column of pixels its own timestamp.

- Visual DNA: Saturated backlit colour streaks on black, compressed to a thin dark horizon and smeared toward the frame edges, with chromatic washes swapping from amber and magenta to cyan, violet, red and green.
- Signature transitions: Slit opening, plane rotation, corridor-to-tunnel fold, white-out flash, slit wipe (time-slice exposure)

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: The infinite zoom is a single unbroken push into an image in which every scene turns out to contain the next, so the camera can travel forever at a constant exponential rate. Charles and Ray Eames fixed its grammar in Powers of Ten (1977, after a 1968 sketch), pulling away from a Chicago picnic by a factor of ten every ten seconds; the Droste effect and Escher's Print Gallery (1956) supplied the recursion, fractal explorers the endless dive, and the online Zoom Quilt (2004) made it a collaborative loop of hand-painted scenes.

- Motion DNA: One continuous push at constant log speed: the field shrinks by a factor of five every two seconds about each portal's fixed point, with a slight roll as each tilted portal straightens, and after five scenes the picture is back where it began — the film loops without a cut.
- Visual DNA: Warm, legible illustration in five idioms — aerial park map, glossy magazine photo, lamplit cabin interior, painterly night city, retro desktop UI — linked by the Powers-of-Ten target square and a white HUD of level and magnification.
- Signature transitions: None: each portal grows to fill the frame and becomes the next scene; the last scene's photo is the first scene
- Key techniques: Nested scene recursion, Exponential camera scale, Fixed-point portal maps

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)

Hugh Blackburn's pendulum of 1844 and Jules Lissajous's optical figures of 1857 led to parlour and lecture-hall instruments, and in 1909 Joseph Goold and his co-authors published Harmonic Vibrations and Vibration Figures, an album of rosettes drawn by twin-elliptic pendulums tuned to musical intervals. It is an ancestor of plotter and generative art: a simple physical rule, run for long enough, makes intricate drawings.

- Motion DNA: Two pendulums released from rest swing in slow ellipses; the pen loops in real time, then time-lapses into a blur while a rosette builds layer on layer, rotates by its slight mistuning and shrinks inward as damping takes the energy out.

- Signature transitions: Draw back and release, pen drop, real time to time-lapse, pen lift, machine slides out, card becomes the plate

## 97 · Pixilation
*Live actors, one frame at a time · 1908 — · Analog, Physical & Stop Motion*

Reference film: `videos/pixilation.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Pixilation** (Live actors, one frame at a time, 1908 —; family: Analog, Physical & Stop Motion).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Pixilation animates real people and objects with the stop-motion camera: actors hold a pose for each exposure, move a little, and hold again, so on screen they glide, levitate and change clothes without ever walking. Émile Cohl and Segundo de Chomón used the trick in the 1900s; Norman McLaren made it an art form at the National Film Board of Canada with Neighbours (1952), which won an Academy Award, and the technique returned in music videos with Peter Gabriel’s Sledgehammer and in the short films of PES.
- Study these reference works: Neighbours (Norman McLaren, NFB, 1952) · A Chairy Tale (Norman McLaren & Claude Jutra, 1957) · Sledgehammer (Peter Gabriel, dir. Stephen R. Johnson, with Aardman and the Brothers Quay, 1986) · Western Spaghetti (PES, 2008) · Fresh Guacamole (PES, 2012)

The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Light painting is drawing in the air with a moving light while the camera's shutter stays open, so every path the light takes is written into a single photograph and the dimly lit performer barely registers. Frank and Lillian Gilbreth traced workers' motions with small lights in the 1910s, Man Ray signed his name in light in Space Writings (1935), and Gjon Mili's 1949 photographs for LIFE of Pablo Picasso drawing centaurs and bulls with a penlight made it famous. Today it is a performance genre of LED wands, pixel sticks and spinning steel wool.
- Study these reference works: Frank & Lillian Gilbreth — light motion studies (1910s) · Man Ray — Space Writings (1935) · Gjon Mili & Pablo Picasso — light drawings for LIFE (1949)
- Motion DNA: Nothing on screen moves except the light and the person carrying it; every path persists, so the image only ever accumulates: a coil grows across the frame, a ring spins up and sprays sparks, and a word is written stroke by stroke until the shutter closes.
- Visual DNA: Near-black blue-hour scene with a wet ground that mirrors the light, saturated RGB ribbon bands, orange spark parabolas with white-hot cores, a warm-white handwritten word, translucent ghosts of the performer, and minimal camera HUD type.
- Signature transitions: Shutter opens, wand coil, walk, steel-wool spin, walk, written word, shutter closes on the finished frame
- Key techniques: Additive exposure buffer, Parabolic spark streaks, Dwell-weighted ribbons

## 109 · Databending

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Databending** (Corrupting the file, not the picture, 2000s —; family: Digital, Internet & Screen).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Databending treats an image or video file as raw data and breaks it on purpose: bytes are overwritten in a hex or text editor, the file is opened as audio and run through effects, or a compressed video loses its keyframes so motion from one shot drags the pixels of another (datamoshing). It grew from circuit bending and net art in the early 2000s; Takeshi Murata’s Monster Movie (2005) and Rosa Menkman’s The Collapse of PAL (2010) and Glitch Moment/um (2011) made the compression artefacts themselves the subject, and datamosh reached music videos in the late 2000s.
- Study these reference works: Monster Movie (Takeshi Murata, 2005) · Untitled (Pink Dot) (Takeshi Murata, 2007) · The Collapse of PAL (Rosa Menkman, 2010) · A Vernacular of File Formats (Rosa Menkman, 2010) · Welcome to Heartbreak (Kanye West, dir. Nabil Elderkin, 2009)
- Motion DNA: Damage propagates in the order the decoder reads: a single changed byte slides everything after it, a deleted keyframe lets the next shot’s motion vectors push the last picture around so pixels bloom, smear and swirl in blocks, and the decay only ever moves forward until a clean keyframe resets it.
- Visual DNA: A real, colourful photograph broken along its compression grid: 8×8 blocks out of step with colour casts, stray DCT stripes, decoder grey where data ran out, blocky macroblock trails, banded rows where audio effects shifted bytes, plus the tools themselves — hex dumps, frame-type strips, a waveform.
- Signature transitions: Block-by-block decode, hex edit with decoder sweep, deleted I-frame into P-frame bleed, raw-audio echo, clean I-frame reset, drip
- Key techniques: JPEG block slip & DC shift, I-frame removal datamosh, Raw-audio echo on RGB bytes

If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Reference film: `videos/surreal.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Surreal Cinema** (Dream logic on film, 1928 —; family: Cinematic & Film Language).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Surrealist film cuts the way a dream does: rooms open onto impossible places, objects turn into other objects and the intertitles lie about time. Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí’s Un Chien Andalou (1929) set the grammar, Maya Deren’s Meshes of the Afternoon (1943) looped a dreamer through her own house, Jan Švankmajer animated objects into uncanny life, and David Lynch carried the mode into curtained rooms with zigzag floors.
- Study these reference works: Un Chien Andalou (Luis Buñuel & Salvador Dalí, 1929) · L’Âge d’Or (Buñuel, 1930) · Meshes of the Afternoon (Maya Deren & Alexander Hammid, 1943) · Spellbound, dream sequence designed by Dalí (Alfred Hitchcock, 1945) · Dimensions of Dialogue (Jan Švankmajer, 1982) · Alice (Švankmajer, 1988) · Twin Peaks (David Lynch & Mark Frost, 1990) · Mulholland Drive (Lynch, 2001)
- Motion DNA: A slow camera that never stops: an even dolly that is suddenly pulled through a door, a tilt from cloud down to sand, a fall into an eye. Things move with dream patience — a key floating, men rising like balloons, a clock sagging — and one object turns into another in stepped stop-motion jumps.
- Visual DNA: Red pleated curtains over a black-and-white zigzag floor, a hooded figure with a mirror for a face, Magritte’s blue sky and sculpted clouds (an eye whose iris is sky, bowler-hatted men, a bird cut from sky, a night street under a noon sky), Dalí’s ochre plain, cliffs and melting clock, soft grain and lying intertitles.
- Signature transitions: Door as portal, tilt reveal, match on object (key becomes bird), a blink, zoom into the pupil as it turns into a keyhole

## 130 · Ukiyo-e Motion
*Woodblock Prints · 1670s — · Cultural & Regional*

Reference film: `videos/ukiyoe.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Ukiyo-e Motion** (Woodblock Prints, 1670s —; family: Cultural & Regional).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Edo-period Japan’s “pictures of the floating world”: a keyblock of black outlines is carved, then one block per colour is inked and rubbed onto damp washi with a baren, so every print is a stack of flat, registered colour layers. Hokusai and Hiroshige made imported Prussian blue and the graded bokashi wipe the look of the 1830s landscape print.
- Study these reference works: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Hokusai, c.1831) · Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (Hokusai, 1830–32) · Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake (Hiroshige, 1857) · One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Hiroshige, 1856–58)
- Motion DNA: The image is pulled block by block like a real print, then moves only in held, graphic poses: the wave curls into its claw-foam peak, boats rock, Hiroshige rain slashes across and the seal lands.
- Visual DNA: Flat registered colour inside confident black keyblock lines, Prussian blue graded into bare paper, with woodgrain and fibre showing through the ink.
- Signature transitions: Block-by-block print pull, registration settle, rain veil, seal stamp
- Key techniques: Keyblock + colour-block layers, Prussian-blue bokashi, Woodgrain & washi texture

## 137 · Minhwa 민화
*Korean Folk Painting · 18th–19th c. — · Cultural & Regional*

Reference film: `videos/minhwa.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Minhwa 민화** (Korean Folk Painting, 18th–19th c. —; family: Cultural & Regional).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: In late Joseon Korea, anonymous itinerant painters made “people’s paintings” for ordinary homes: magpie-and-tiger pictures to ward off evil at New Year, chaekgeori bookshelf screens, peonies for wealth and the ten symbols of longevity. Flat mineral colour, firm ink outlines and a cheerfully foolish tiger set them apart from court painting; Yanagi Muneyoshi championed them, and the 2018 PyeongChang Olympic mascot Soohorang descends from that tiger.
- Study these reference works: Magpie and Tiger (Kkachi Horangi), 19th c., Leeum Museum of Art · Chaekgeori screens attributed to Yi Eung-rok (19th c.) · Sipjangsaeng ten-longevity screens (Joseon court and folk) · Moran-do peony screens · Soohorang, PyeongChang 2018 mascot
- Motion DNA: Paper-cut-out stiffness with comic timing: the tiger pops up on a spring and rolls its huge eyes, the magpie hops and caws, peonies burst open, and screen panels unfold in a zigzag.
- Visual DNA: Outlined, flattened forms in vermilion, ochre, malachite and indigo on yellowed hanji: a striped-and-spotted grinning tiger under a pine, a black-and-white magpie, scalloped peonies and stylised rocks.

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Byzantine Mosaic** (Gold glass and tesserae, 5th–15th c.; family: Cultural & Regional).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Byzantine mosaic builds images from tesserae, small cubes of stone and coloured glass, set in rows that follow the forms they describe (andamento) over grounds of gold-leaf glass that glint as the light or the viewer moves. In Ravenna the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia (c. 425–450) has a deep blue vault strewn with gold stars and San Vitale (c. 547) shows the court of Justinian and Theodora; the Deësis panel in Hagia Sophia (c. 1261) reached a painterly softness with very small tesserae.
- Study these reference works: Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, Ravenna (c. 425–450) · San Vitale, Justinian and Theodora panels, Ravenna (c. 547) · Hagia Sophia, Deësis panel, Constantinople (c. 1261) · Chora Church (Kariye), Constantinople (c. 1315–1321)
- Motion DNA: Accumulation, then light. Tiles are pressed in singly at first and then faster and faster in waves that run along their rows, outward from the figure; when the surface is whole nothing moves but a lamp, and the gold answers it tile by tile with glints that flicker on and off as the angle passes.
- Visual DNA: Small irregular squares with dark grout between; gold-glass ground laid in rows that halo the figure; a blue and green peacock with a dark outline row and eyed tail, vine scrolls with leaves and grapes, a deep lapis vault with eight-pointed gold stars under a red and white arch, a border of red with white diamonds and pearl beading; red-ochre sinopia on plaster where nothing is set yet.
- Signature transitions: Close-up pulls back as the surface fills; a lamp sweep; the title set in gold on the vault
- Key techniques: Rows follow the forms (andamento), Tilted gold smalti glint, Tesserae set one by one

- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.

- Suggested tools: Stone and gold- or colour-backed glass tesserae pressed into lime mortar over a painted sinopia, Canvas 2D: label masks, a distance field per region, greedy tile packing along its iso-lines, Per-tile tilt vectors for specular glints. The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Destruction effects break a solid into pieces and hand them to a rigid-body solver. James O’Brien and Jessica Hodgins simulated brittle fracture from stress in 1999 (ductile fracture followed in 2002); production and games mostly pre-fracture instead, cutting the model into Voronoi cells around scattered points, as in Houdini’s Voronoi Fracture, 3ds Max RayFire and Blender’s Cell Fracture, while Pixelux’s Digital Molecular Matter and Volition’s GeoMod brought dynamic breakage to consoles.
- Study these reference works: Star Wars: The Force Unleashed (LucasArts, 2008; Pixelux DMM) · Red Faction: Guerrilla (Volition, 2009; GeoMod 2.0) · Teardown (Tuxedo Labs, 2020)
- Motion DNA: A beat of stillness, a heavy ball arcs in and connects on the downbeat; time drops to a quarter speed as the cracks open, then catches up while shards spray, spin and rain down, bouncing and skidding to rest. ## 175 · Overshoot
*One pass past the target, then settle · 1930s — · Technique Atlas*

Reference film: `videos/techovershoot.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Overshoot** (One pass past the target, then settle, 1930s —; family: Technique Atlas).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Disney animators taught overshoot as part of follow-through: a move carries past its final pose and eases back into it, so it reads as having weight and energy. In software it became the “back” easing curve — Robert Penner’s easing equations (2001) defined easeOutBack with its overshoot constant 1.70158, about a 10% overshoot — and that curve now ships in CSS cubic-bezier presets, GSAP’s back.out and nearly every animation library.
- Study these reference works: The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation (Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, 1981; follow-through and overlapping action) · Robert Penner’s Easing Equations (Flash ActionScript, 2001) · GSAP back.out ease (GreenSock)
- Motion DNA: Every move takes one second: a fast start, a single excursion past the target, a turn and a soft settle — no second swing. Five lanes compare strengths from none (plain cubic ease-out) to s = 4 (about 38% past); they return on the next bar, overshooting the start mark; then the same curve drives a pop-in scale, a quarter-turn and a slide, with MOTION sliding in a beat behind.
- Visual DNA: The Technique Atlas stage; five lanes of small orange Tokens on thin tracks between dashed START and TARGET lines; dashed ghosts at each peak with a bracket and the measured overshoot; then one large Token with a dashed target outline, an angle arc with target and peak ticks, and target lines for the slide; all five curves faint in the caption graph with the active one in ink.
- Signature transitions: Lane race into a hero Token; overshoot on scale, rotation and position
- Key techniques: Ease-out-back curve, Overshoot strength s, Single pass, no oscillation

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Ease-out-back curve, Overshoot strength s, Single pass, no oscillation).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Ease-out-back curve and a signature transition.

```text

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Changing the speed of time on screen is as old as the hand-cranked camera: overcranking gave slow motion, undercranking fast motion, and early filmmakers ran film backwards for reverse. Optical printers could hold frames for a freeze or skip them, and the closing freeze of Truffaut’s The 400 Blows (1959) made the held frame famous. Digital editing turned it into a curve: Adobe After Effects’ Time Remapping maps output time to source time per frame, and speed ramps became a staple of music videos and action films after The Matrix (1999).
- Study these reference works: The 400 Blows / Les Quatre Cents Coups (François Truffaut, 1959; final freeze frame) · The Matrix (The Wachowskis, 1999) · 300 (Zack Snyder, 2007; speed ramps)
- Motion DNA: The source clip is an even, regular hop; all the expression comes from the clock. Two seconds at 100%, a one-second ease into 20%, a hard hold at 4.5 s, a cut into −100% reverse at 5.5 s, a ramp through zero up to 250% and a final ease back to 100% — so the same hop reads as floaty, frozen, rewound and frantic.
- Visual DNA: The Technique Atlas stage with its floor line: the orange Token hopping across a dotted path, six outlined ghosts at fixed output intervals, an ink arrow showing source velocity; a source ruler under the floor with a playhead and source-frame counter; a speed graph and a large speed percentage top right; the remap curve (source time over output time) as the caption graph.
- Signature transitions: Speed ramps, a hold (freeze frame), a hard cut into reverse
- Key techniques: Keyed speed integrated to a remap curve, Freeze as a hold, Reverse as negative speed

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Keyed speed integrated to a remap curve, Freeze as a hold, Reverse as negative speed).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Keyed speed integrated to a remap curve and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "TIME REMAPPING", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: Over- and undercranked cameras, optical-printer step printing, After Effects Time Remapping / Premiere and Resolve speed ramps, Canvas 2D: keyed speed integrated in setup() into a source-time table. ### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Particles** (Emit, age, die, 1982 —; family: Technique Atlas).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: William T. Reeves at Lucasfilm defined the particle system for the Genesis Effect in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982) and described it in Particle Systems — A Technique for Modeling a Class of Fuzzy Objects (SIGGRAPH 1983): emitters generate particles with a birth rate, each gets an initial position, velocity, colour, size and lifetime, moves under simple forces and is killed when its age runs out. The same emit-update-kill loop drives Maya and Houdini particles, Trapcode Particular in After Effects and every game engine’s effects system.

Then the anchor descends, the Token lands and stands, and the rope folds down onto the floor and settles.

The holds lag the smooth ghost and jump to catch up, biggest jumps in the middle of the ease. Then a 6 fps stop-motion run of rolls and hops that never sits quite still between poses, and a word set letter by letter on the same clock.

- Motion DNA: Clean holds, then one bar of breakage per transition: the glitch amount swells and decays across eight sixteenths, jumping to a new seeded value on each one, with the hard cut landing on the beat in the middle where the damage is worst. Four operations arrive one transition at a time — channels split, slices shift, rows tear, blocks freeze and drag — and the last transition stacks all four before the final state settles clean.
- Visual DNA: The Technique Atlas stage with the picture framed in ink at the centre; Token states in orange, ink, blue and paper colourways; red and blue fringes, sideways-shifted bands, torn scanlines and a coarse block mosaic; a left-hand operation stack with live parameters and amount bars; slice and row offset charts on the right aligned to the picture; a sixteenth-note amount strip with the cut under the picture.
- Signature transitions: Glitch cuts: RGB split, block displacement, scanline tear, quantise hold, then all four stacked
- Key techniques: RGB channel offset, Seeded slice displacement, Quantised datamosh hold

- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (RGB channel offset, Seeded slice displacement, Quantised datamosh hold).

- Lineage: Panning, short for panorama, arrived when cameras were first mounted on heads that could turn: early actuality films around 1896–1900 swept across crowds and landscapes, and geared and later fluid heads made smooth pans and tilts routine. Cinematographers’ handbooks such as the American Cinematographer Manual give pan-speed tables; the common rule of thumb is that an object should take about seven seconds to cross the frame.

- Lineage: A whip pan (also swish or flash pan) swings the camera so quickly that the frame dissolves into horizontal streaks. ```text

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Craig Reynolds introduced boids in “Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model” at SIGGRAPH 1987: each agent sees only nearby flockmates and steers by separation, alignment and cohesion, and flocking emerges with nobody choreographing it. The method went straight into film crowds — the bat swarms and penguins of Batman Returns (1992) — and later into dedicated crowd and swarm tools such as Massive and Houdini’s crowd and POP solvers.

- Motion DNA: Disorder becoming order one rule at a time, on the beat: with no rules the Tokens wander and cross; separation spaces them out; alignment turns them into parallel streams; cohesion pulls the streams into flocks that bank together at the walls. A big Token then dives through the flock, which bursts open around it and closes behind; once it leaves, the flock re-forms.
- Visual DNA: The Technique Atlas stage with 120 small orange Tokens, each rotated to its heading and trailing a faint line of its last frames; one inked boid with its dashed neighbour and separation radii, thin links to its neighbours and colour-coded steering arrows; a rule panel with switches; the big predator Token with its flee radius.
- Signature transitions: Rules switch on at 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 s; predator in at 6.5 s, breaks off at 8.6 s and leaves frame
- Key techniques: Neighbour radius 120 px, separation 44 px, Steering = Σ weighted rule forces, clamped speed, Predator: flee force inside 320 px

- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.

- Lineage: Forward kinematics poses a chain joint by joint; inverse kinematics runs the other way, solving the joint angles that put the end of the chain on a goal. Finally a three-bone arm solves on the beat, one iteration per beat, snapping closer each time, then tracks the Token smoothly.

- Lineage: Takeo Igarashi, Tomer Moscovich and John F. Hughes introduced As-Rigid-As-Possible Shape Manipulation at SIGGRAPH 2005: a 2D shape is triangulated, the user drags a few handles, and a least-squares solve keeps every triangle as close as possible to a rotated copy of itself, so the figure bends instead of shearing. Olga Sorkine and Marc Alexa’s local/global ARAP solver (2007), used here, is the iteration most later tools follow.

A rigid copy beside it cannot reach the pins; a linear blend reaches them but squeezes the hole. With the area around the hole starched, the same drag bends only the lower half. Finally the word MOTION, rigged as one strip, is arched and waved by three pins.

- Lineage: Alan Turing’s The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952) showed that two diffusing, reacting chemicals can break a uniform field into spots and stripes. Peter Gray and Stephen K. Pearson’s Complex Patterns in a Simple System (Science, 1993) mapped its feed and kill parameters into a zoo of regimes. - Motion DNA: Nothing is animated by hand: a dashed outline of the Token is poured into three dishes on the first downbeat and the equations take over. Slowly at first, then faster as more steps run per frame, the outline swells and breaks — into dots that split and pack the dish, into parallel bands that echo the Token’s corners outward, into a branching coral maze. One dish is spotlit every two bars while its point lights up on the F–k map.

## 214 · L-System
*Rewrite a string, then let a turtle draw it · 1968 — · Technique Atlas*

Reference film: `videos/techlsystem.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **L-System** (Rewrite a string, then let a turtle draw it, 1968 —; family: Technique Atlas).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: The biologist Aristid Lindenmayer introduced L-systems in 1968 to describe how cells of simple organisms divide: every symbol of a string is rewritten at once by its rule. Alvy Ray Smith drew plants from them in Plants, Fractals, and Formal Languages (SIGGRAPH 1984), and Przemysław Prusinkiewicz gave them the turtle interpretation — F forward, + and − turn, brackets push and pop a branch — used ever since, collected with Lindenmayer in The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants (1990). Procedural tools such as Houdini’s L-system node grow trees, ivy and growth animations the same way.
- Study these reference works: Plants, Fractals, and Formal Languages (Alvy Ray Smith, SIGGRAPH 1984) · The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants (Przemysław Prusinkiewicz & Aristid Lindenmayer, Springer, 1990) · L-System node in Houdini (SideFX)
- Motion DNA: Growth by generations on the downbeat: each new string is read left to right by a turtle whose path appears as it goes, so the stem climbs first and every branch flicks out in reading order; the previous generation stays underneath as a ghost the new one traces over. After the fifth generation the branching angle snaps on three beats — narrower, wider, back — and the whole plant re-folds at once, buds and all.
- Visual DNA: The Technique Atlas stage; ink stems thinning with branch depth, small orange Tokens as buds at every X and a few larger accent Tokens as flowers; left, the axiom, the two rules and the angle in mono type, a table of generations with string lengths, and a read-head window that highlights the symbol the turtle is on.
- Signature transitions: Each generation grows over the ghost of the last; the angle re-sets with a springy overshoot
- Key techniques: Parallel rewriting: X → F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X, F → FF, Turtle: F draw, ± turn δ, [ ] push / pop, Step halves each generation so the skeleton is kept

- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "L-SYSTEM", held for about 1 s.

It ends on a clean title card reading "BLOOM". Punchy sound design synced to every cut.

A tracked sample on the sphere slides across the matcap inset as the camera moves, its leader line linking the surface to the pixel it reads.
- Visual DNA: A dark sculpt-viewport backdrop with a soft centre glow; objects shaded entirely from the painted sphere, the floor only darkened by contact occlusion, so there are no cast shadows. Top right: the matcap sphere with a crosshair at the lookup point; under it a view-space normal pass. Mono readouts give N·right, N·up and the uv they become.
- Signature transitions: Split wipe from the plain render; short crossfades between matcaps on the beat
- Key techniques: View-space normal lookup, Painted lit sphere, Lights baked, camera-locked

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)

## 227 · Ambient Occlusion

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Ambient Occlusion** (How much sky each point can see, 2001 —; family: Rendering Looks).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Ambient occlusion approximates the soft darkening of creases and contact points under even sky light by measuring how open each point is, without simulating full global illumination. Zhukov, Iones and Kronin described the related idea of obscurances in 1998; Hayden Landis and colleagues at ILM brought ambient occlusion into feature production around Pearl Harbor (2001) and documented it in the SIGGRAPH 2002 course on production global illumination. The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Fog is the oldest depth cue in real-time graphics: the image is blended toward a fog colour by a function of distance, so far geometry fades into the backdrop instead of popping at the far clip plane. Flight simulators used it from the 1980s, and fixed-function OpenGL (1992) and Direct3D standardised three modes — linear, exponential and exponential-squared — computed per vertex or per pixel from eye depth. Height-dependent fog, which integrates a density that thins with altitude along the view ray, became common in game engines in the 2000s; modern engines extend it to volumetric fog that also scatters light.
- Study these reference works: Silent Hill (Konami, 1999; fog as atmosphere and draw-distance cover) · Turok: Dinosaur Hunter (Iguana Entertainment, 1997; distance fog on the Nintendo 64) · Limbo (Playdead, 2010; layered depth haze)

## 232 · Film Grain & Halation

The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Film grain is the visible clumping of silver halide crystals and dye clouds in the emulsion; it is strongest in the midtones and changes every frame because every frame is a new piece of film. Halation is the red-orange glow around bright edges where light passes through the emulsion, reflects off the film base and re-exposes the red-sensitive layer from behind; anti-halation backings suppress it, and stocks without one show it strongly. Gate weave is the slight frame-to-frame drift of film in the camera and projector gate. As digital cameras replaced film, finishing tools added these artefacts back on purpose, from scanned grain plates to procedural emulations.
- Study these reference works: Dune (Denis Villeneuve, 2021; shot digitally, recorded out to film and scanned back for its texture) · Euphoria season 2 (HBO, 2022; shot on Kodak Ektachrome) · Dehancer (film-emulation plug-in modelling grain, halation and bloom)
- Motion DNA: The camera makes the shared 50° orbit while the finish builds on the beat: grain fades in and starts boiling at 30 frames a second, the halation threshold glow rises until the rim-lit edges bleed red, the gate begins to weave and the vignette closes in; a split then shows the clean render against the finish before the whole frame returns to film.
- Visual DNA: A low-key version of the still life: black studio, one hard key and a rim light that rings each object in white, each ring haloed in red-orange; fine monochrome grain alive in the midtones, quiet in the blacks; soft dark corners. Insets show the grain plate and the halation pass; a loupe magnifies a rim edge at 3×; mono readouts give grain σ, frame seed, threshold, halation strength, weave and vignette.
- Signature transitions: Effects layered on one by one; a split against the clean render

- Lineage: Robert Hooke described the colours of thin plates in Micrographia (1665), and Isaac Newton measured them in Opticks (1704) — Newton’s rings, where colour follows the thickness of a film of air. - Motion DNA: The shared camera orbit sweeps the view angle across every surface, so bands of colour slide over the bevels of the Token and round the bubble as the camera moves. A wipe turns the plain paper studio into a dark set with a soap-bubble sphere and a beetle-shell Token; the film thickness then steps on the beat (420 → 250 → 560 → 780 → 430 nm), recolouring both at once, and the thickness noise grows from ±70 to ±170 nm while the bubble’s film drains and swirls faster.
- Visual DNA: A near-black studio with softbox reflections: a nearly invisible bubble drawn only by its reflections — magenta, gold, green and blue bands, darker at the thin top, the softboxes doubled on the front and back walls — and a dark Token whose lacquer glows through gold, violet and teal with angle. An interference-colour chart as the thickness ruler, a hue-vs-angle strip, thickness and view-angle passes.
- Signature transitions: Wipe from the plain studio to the dark set; beat-stepped film thickness; thickness noise ramp
- Key techniques: Two-beam Airy reflectance per λ, Spectral → RGB via CIE fits, LUT d × θ, Thickness noise, draining, swirl

## 244 · Chromatic Aberration
*Colours that refuse to meet: lens fringing in post · 1700s optics · 2000s — as a look · Rendering Looks*

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text

The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Glass bends short wavelengths more than long ones (dispersion), so a simple lens brings blue to a focus closer than red. Isaac Newton concluded in Opticks (1704) that this colour error could not be removed from lenses, one reason he built a reflecting telescope. It was corrected in the 18th century by the achromatic doublet, a converging crown-glass lens paired with a diverging flint-glass one: Chester Moor Hall made the first ones in the 1730s and John Dollond patented and sold them from 1758. Real-time renderers later added the fringe back on purpose as a post effect that imitates imperfect camera lenses, often next to grain and vignetting.
- Study these reference works: Isaac Newton, Opticks (1704) · John Dollond’s achromatic doublet (patented 1758) · Alien: Isolation (Creative Assembly, 2014; lens fringing with grain for a 1970s-film look)
- Motion DNA: The shared 10 s camera move: a 50° orbit with a slight drift down while the Token bobs and turns. A wipe brings in the uncorrected lens; on each beat the lateral scale steps up (R ×1.006 → ×1.0185 with B scaled down the same) so the fringes widen toward the frame edges; then longitudinal blur grows on R and B; finally a wipe from the right corrects the lens with a doublet and holds as a split, uncorrected on the left.
- Visual DNA: The plain still life with red and cyan-blue fringes along every silhouette, near zero at the centre and widest at the cube and sphere, then soft purple-green halos on all edges; on the corrected side, clean edges. A loupe with the edge’s pixels and its R, G, B profile, concentric rings giving the fringe width at each radius, and a ray diagram of three wavelengths focusing apart.
- Signature transitions: Wipe from the ideal lens to the aberrated one; stepped strength on the beat; a wipe to the corrected lens holding as a split
- Key techniques: Lateral CA: per-channel radial scale, Longitudinal CA: R and B defocused, Achromatic doublet as the correction

The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Printing presses cannot print grey: a spot either takes ink or it does not, so continuous tone is broken into dots whose size follows the tone. Photographic halftone screens appeared in the 1880s — Frederic Ives in Philadelphia and Georg Meisenbach in Munich were among their inventors — and newspapers adopted them for photographs around 1900. Colour printing separates the image into cyan, magenta, yellow and black and gives each its own screen angle, conventionally 15°, 75°, 0° and 45°, so the grids form a small rosette instead of a visible moiré. Stochastic or FM screening, which keeps one tiny dot size and varies how many there are, came with digital imagesetters in the 1990s.
- Study these reference works: Roy Lichtenstein, Drowning Girl (1963; Ben-Day dots enlarged into the image) · Sigmar Polke, raster paintings (1960s; enlarged halftone dots) · Into the Spider-Verse (Sony Pictures Animation, 2018; halftone shading in an animated feature)
- Motion DNA: The camera makes the shared 50° orbit. A wipe prints the plain render into four dot screens; the separations and the screen-angle diagram come up, and the screen ruling steps finer on each beat — 20, 14, 10, 7.5 px cells — before settling at 12 for a loupe on the rosette. Then the press runs one ink only: AM dots fill the frame, and a wipe brings in FM stochastic dots for the right half, with a loupe straddling the line.
- Visual DNA: Warm newsprint paper; the orange Token as overlapping magenta and yellow dots, the blue cube as cyan and magenta, shadows built from black dots at 45°, every dot a vector circle that sharpens under the loupe. Paper panels hold the readouts, the four separation plates in their inks, the source render and a protractor of the four screen angles; the coda is black ink alone, ordered dots on the left, grainy stochastic dots on the right.
- Signature transitions: Wipe from the plain render to print; hard cut on the beat to one ink; split AM | FM
- Key techniques: CMYK separation, 70 % black replacement, Screens at C 15° · M 75° · Y 0° · K 45°, AM dots vs FM error diffusion

## 248 · Title Sequence
*Opening credits in order, held to be read · 1950s — · Narrative Formats*

Reference film: `videos/formattitles.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Title Sequence** (Opening credits in order, held to be read, 1950s —; family: Narrative Formats).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Early sound films opened on static title cards. In the mid-1950s Saul Bass turned the opening credits into a designed sequence, starting with Carmen Jones (1954) and The Man with the Golden Arm (1955), and the title sequence became its own craft — Maurice Binder’s Bond openings from Dr. No (1962), Pablo Ferro, and later Kyle Cooper’s Se7en (1995). The order of the credits themselves is set largely by guild agreements and contracts: distributor and production company first, the possessory credit, the stars, the main title, the key crew, and the director last.

## 260 · Timeline
*History told as a camera move along one axis · 1765 — · Narrative Formats*

Reference film: `videos/formattimeline.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Timeline** (History told as a camera move along one axis, 1765 —; family: Narrative Formats).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: The timeline as a picture of history goes back to Joseph Priestley’s A Chart of Biography (1765), which drew lives as bars on a single scaled time axis, and his New Chart of History (1769). Television documentaries and museum films turned it into a camera move: a line travelling across the frame, dates rolling past, an event card at each stop. Web and motion explainers made it a template — the horizontal scroll, the milestone card on a stem, the jump to “today” — and with it a choice every timeline makes: even steps, one per event, or scaled time, where gaps are as long as the years they hold.
- Study these reference works: Joseph Priestley, A Chart of Biography (1765) · Charles Joseph Minard and later infographic history charts in print · Knight Lab TimelineJS (Northwestern University, 2012 —) used across web journalism
- Motion DNA: A short title, then the camera dollies along the axis in hold-and-move steps, arriving on every second beat so each milestone card can spring out on its stem while the next marker waits off to the right. At the turn the camera pulls back to show the whole line, the gaps between events are labelled in years, and the evenly spaced markers slide to their true positions in scaled time. Then a push in on the present, where the Token and MOTION land.
- Visual DNA: The Technique Atlas paper stage; one ink axis with round markers; cream cards with an ink keyline, an orange edge bar, a heavy year and a mono line, each with a small drawing of the Token at that stage (sharp square, rounded square, punched hole, orange, turning). Decade ticks appear only in scaled time; a small EVEN | SCALED switch and a FICTIONAL CHRONOLOGY note sit under the structure strip.
- Signature transitions: Camera dolly between stops; pull-back and re-spacing of the axis; push-in to the present
- Key techniques: Milestone cards on stems, Even steps vs. scaled time, Zoom to the present

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)
- 0.0–1.5 s  Hook: open on the single most recognisable element of the style.
- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Milestone cards on stems, Even steps vs. scaled time, Zoom to the present).
- 5.0–8.0 s  Climax: the most spectacular moment, built on Milestone cards on stems and a signature transition.
- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "TIMELINE", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: After Effects null-driven camera on a long precomp, Web scroll timelines (TimelineJS, scrollytelling), Canvas 2D: one world transform per frame (camera x, zoom), markers lerped between even and scaled x. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. Make each frame a pure function of time t, and use seeded randomness so any frame can be re-rendered exactly.
- Sound is part of the film: write a score and sound effects whose hits land exactly on the visual events. Keep peaks below 0 dBFS.
- Use the style's real palette, materials and typography, and include at least one detail that only this style would have.
- One-shot: it does not need to loop.
- Reproducibility note: Fully procedural (the chronology is invented).

DELIVER: the film (or code that renders it), plus a beat sheet listing each event with its timing.
```

Every cut lands on a bar of the 120 BPM bed.

## 265 · Ad-break Bumper
*We’ll be right back · now back to · 1950s — · Narrative Formats*

Reference film: `videos/formatbumper.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Ad-break Bumper** (We’ll be right back · now back to, 1950s —; family: Narrative Formats).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Commercial television split its programmes into acts around advertising from the start, and short station or programme idents either side of the break — bumpers — marked where the show stopped and resumed. In the US the FCC’s 1974 policy on children’s television required a separation device around the ads in children’s programmes, which made bumpers a fixture of Saturday-morning cartoons; Japanese anime has its own version in the mid-episode eyecatch. Cartoon Network’s and Adult Swim’s bumps from the late 1990s and 2000s turned the form into a showcase. Writers end each act on a hook — the act out — and the act in often repeats its last beat.
- Study these reference works: Saturday-morning cartoon bumpers (US, 1970s–90s) · Cowboy Bebop (1998; eyecatches) · Adult Swim bumps (2001 —)
- Motion DNA: The act runs to a freeze at 1.25 s and dips to black; the out-bumper wipes in at 1.6 s, its logo loop on half-second beats, ending on an unresolved chord; the break runs compressed ×35, five spots in 3.4 s, each with its own jingle and a black frame between; the in-bumper at 6.4 s plays the same loop and resolves; the act in at 7.8 s replays the teeter and goes on — the catch lands at about 9.15 s.
- Visual DNA: The show on the paper stage: an ink table, a blue cube tipping off its edge, the orange Token. Bumpers as full-bleed orange (out) and blue (in) cards with MOTION and the hopping Token. The break in master-control grey: a monitor with generic spots, the pod as a slot timeline with :15 / :30 labels, a big mono break clock. A rundown of the half hour top right, a translucent logo bug bottom right.
- Signature transitions: Freeze and dip to black out of the act; hard wipes in and out of the bumpers; a black frame between spots; a straight cut back into the act
- Key techniques: Act out on a hook, dip to black, Out- and in-bumper: logo, one line, a short loop, Act in repeats the last beat; logo bug on

FILM STRUCTURE (10.0 s · 1920×1080 · 30 fps)

- 1.5–5.0 s  Development: bring in the signature techniques one at a time (Act out on a hook, dip to black, Out- and in-bumper: logo, one line, a short loop, Act in repeats the last beat; logo bug on).

- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "AD-BREAK BUMPER", held for about 1 s.

- Suggested tools: Network presentation package: bumpers, logo bug, break format, Playout automation inserts the pod between the bumpers, Canvas 2D: one show rig driven by story time, a pod table driving monitor, timeline and clock. If you write code, make everything procedural (Canvas 2D or WebGL for picture, Web Audio for sound) with no external assets. The Token barely moves: small pulses on the syllables.

- Lineage: Unboxing videos grew up on YouTube in the mid-2000s with gadget launches — fans filmed themselves opening the first iPhone in June 2007 — and by 2010 ‘unboxing’ was a genre of its own. The grammar is consistent: an overhead or over-the-shoulder camera, the sealed box shown first, the tape cut and the layers removed one by one, a deliberately slow last layer before the product, then the contents laid out and a first-impression verdict. Brands answered with packaging designed to be filmed — Apple’s nested boxes and pull tabs — and the laid-out contents borrow knolling, Andrew Kromelow’s 1987 habit at Frank Gehry’s furniture shop of arranging tools at right angles, popularised by Tom Sachs.
- Study these reference works: iPhone launch unboxings (YouTube, June 2007) · Unbox Therapy (Lewis Hilsenteger, 2010 —) · Tom Sachs, ‘Ten Bullets’ (2010; ‘Always be knolling’)
- Motion DNA: Action gets shorter then stops: the box drops with a thud, the tape cut runs 0.8 s, the flaps 0.75 s, the lid lifts off in 0.5 s — then the sticker and two tissue sheets take 1.55 s on a slow ease with the music pulled out. The reveal at 5.45 s is a hit, a shine sweep and a 10 % push-in; the box slides aside and five items fly to their knolled spots, alternate hands, one every 0.38 s; the verdict card stamps down at 8.9 s and the Token hops.
- Visual DNA: Top-down light-oak desk; a kraft shipping box with a white label, barcode, red FRAGILE and this-side-up arrows; an off-white inner box with MOTION on the lid, white tissue sealed with an orange sticker, black foam cradling the orange Token. - Signature transitions: One continuous overhead take; a push-in on the reveal and back out for the layout
- Key techniques: Overhead locked-off camera, hands in frame, Each layer slower; the last layer before the reveal slowest, Knolled contents and a first-impression verdict

- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "UNBOXING", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: Overhead rig (camera on a C-stand arm or copy stand) and diffused top light, Real-time capture with a slowed reveal; knolling laid out by hand on a grid, Canvas 2D: fold transforms for flaps and tissue, keyed hand tracks, a pace curve in the caption. ## 269 · Skippable Pre-roll

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Pre-roll — the video ad that plays before the clip a viewer chose — spread with online video in the late 2000s. In 2010 YouTube introduced TrueView in-stream ads, which can be skipped after five seconds and which the advertiser pays for only when the viewer watches 30 seconds (or the whole of a shorter ad) or clicks. The skip line rewrote the structure of the spot: brand and hook front-loaded into the five unskippable seconds, the rest written as a reward for the people who stay. GEICO’s “Unskippable” (The Martin Agency, 2015) made the whole ad fit before the button and won the Film Grand Prix at Cannes Lions.

- Motion DNA: No fade in: frame one already holds the MOTION wordmark as the Token slams down beside it; the lockup shrinks to a brand bug at 1.5 s and the Token hops the one-line pitch on the beat while the skip box counts 5-4-3-2-1; at 5 s it pops into SKIP AD, the audience grid empties, a cursor hovers… and leaves; ‘Still here?’, then a ring of Tokens orbits and collapses into one big Token for the stayers; the end card lands at 8.5 s with the offer and LEARN MORE.

- Signature transitions: Lockup shrinks into a brand bug; hard cuts inside the ad on the skip line and into the payoff; skip box pops from countdown to button; the end card scales in
- Key techniques: Brand and the whole pitch inside the unskippable 5 s, The player is the frame: Ad badge, yellow bar, skip box, Second half written as a payoff for stayers

- 8.0–10.0 s Resolve: a composed final frame with a small title "SKIPPABLE PRE-ROLL", held for about 1 s.

BUILD RULES
- Suggested tools: Edit to the platform’s skip point: brand in shot 1, message complete by 0:05, Second half cut as a reward cut-down; CTA overlay and end screen in the ad platform, Canvas 2D: the ad drawn on a virtual 1920 × 1080 frame scaled into a player mock. ## 270 · Sale Countdown
*Offer, anchor price, scarcity, deadline, CTA · 1900s — · online 2000s — · Narrative Formats*

Reference film: `videos/formatsale.mp4`

### Build prompt (Claude / any coding model / a motion designer)
```text
You are the director, motion designer, engineer and sound designer of ONE 10-second motion-design film in the style of **Sale Countdown** (Offer, anchor price, scarcity, deadline, CTA, 1900s — · online 2000s —; family: Narrative Formats).
The goal is the most classic, yet most stunning reading of this style: award-shortlist / high-end commercial quality. A clean, template-looking result is a fail.

STYLE BRIEF
- Lineage: Sale advertising is as old as the department store, and its devices have names. The struck-through original price is an anchor — Tversky and Kahneman described anchoring in 1974 — and limited stock and a closing deadline are the scarcity principle Robert Cialdini set out in Influence (1984). E-commerce made both live: deal-a-day sites such as Woot (2004) and Amazon’s Lightning Deals put a ticking clock and a claimed-stock bar beside the price, and shopping events such as Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day (first held on 15 July 2015) turned the countdown into the whole ad, with the conditions in the small print at the end.
- Study these reference works: Amazon Prime Day Lightning Deals (2015 —) · Woot deal-a-day (2004 —) · Black Friday doorbuster ads (US retail)

- Lineage: Side-by-side product comparison began in print: Consumers Union’s Consumer Reports (from 1936) rated rival products against the same criteria in the same table, and comparative advertising grew on American television after the FTC encouraged it in 1972 — the Pepsi Challenge (1975) turned it into a blind taste test with a score. Car television made the round-by-round head-to-head a format — Top Gear’s challenges, and the drag races and spec sheets of the web reviews that followed — and YouTube tech channels such as MKBHD and Linus Tech Tips settled its modern grammar: split screen, the same tests in the same order, a running score, and a verdict that usually says what it depends on.

- Motion DNA: A 1.4 s face-off: both contenders slide in from their edges, the VS badge slams at 0.8 s and the four criteria drop into the table.
